ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Two ecologists, Peter and Rosemary Grant, spent thirty years observing, tagging, and measuring finches (a type of bird) in the Galápagos Islands. They made their observations on Daphne Major—one of the most desolate of the Galápagos Islands. It is an uninhabited volcanic cone where only low to the ground cacti and shrubs grow. During 1977, there was a severe drought and seeds of all kinds became scarce. The small, soft seeds were quickly eaten by the birds, leaving mainly large, tough seeds that the finches normally ignore. The year after the drought, the Grants discovered that the average width of the finches' beak had increased.
Which of the following statements best explains the increase in beak size?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text: Finches with larger beaks were able to eat the tougher seeds and were healthier and reproduced more offspring that inherited the trait for wider beaks.

During the 1977 drought on Daphne Major, small soft seeds became scarce, leaving mainly large, tough seeds. The year after the drought, the Grants discovered that the average width of the finches' beaks had increased. Why did the average beak width increase after the drought?
ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_answer: Finches with larger beaks were able to eat the tougher seeds and were healthier and reproduced more offspring that inherited the trait for wider beaks
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows two finch heads labeled “Before” and “After.” The “After” finch is drawn with a visibly wider/deeper beak than the “Before” finch, matching the stated observation that average beak width increased after the drought. Reasoning: The drought acted as an environmental selection pressure. Because small, soft seeds became scarce and mostly large, tough seeds remained, finches with inherited wider/larger beaks were better able to crack and eat the available seeds. These birds were more likely to survive, stay healthy, and reproduce. Their offspring inherited the wider-beak trait, making wider beaks more common in the population and increasing the average beak width.
